# Spectrum and the nature of colour (`spectrum_colour`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/physics.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Physics, optics & astronomy (`physics`)
- Deps: helped by refraction_optics, clear_glass
- Core idea: White sunlight is a mixture of all colours. A narrow beam from a hole in the shutter of a dark room, passed through a triangular glass prism, spreads into a band from red to violet because each colour is bent by a different amount. The decisive test: let one colour from the band pass through a second prism; it is bent again but not split or changed. A lens or a reversed prism brings the colours back together to white. The rainbow is the same effect in raindrops: light is refracted, reflected once inside the drop and refracted again, and comes back at about 42 degrees from the point opposite the Sun.
- Pitfalls:
  - Saying the prism adds or creates the colours (the view Newton refuted)
  - Insisting on exactly seven colours; the band is continuous and Newton's seven follow a musical analogy
  - Confusing mixing of lights (all give white) with mixing of pigments (give dark brown)
  - Screen too close to the prism: the band needs several metres to spread
- History: islamic: c. 1300–1309 – Kamal al-Din al-Farisi explains the rainbow with a water-filled glass sphere; europe: c. 1304–1310 – Theodoric of Freiberg, same explanation independently; 1637 Descartes computes the rainbow angle; 1666–1672 Newton's prism experiments; 1704 Opticks; china: 11th c. – Shen Kuo and Sun Sikong ascribe the rainbow to sunlight in raindrops
- Read:
  - Isaac Newton, Opticks (1704)
  - Carl B. Boyer, The Rainbow: From Myth to Mathematics (1959)
